column4: The section's root م ث ل calls Iram peerless; this ayah says there is nothing like God (لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِۦ شَىْءٌ) and immediately names mates and animal pairs, setting created pairing against the Creator's unlikeness.
The section's root ء ح د is glossed in 89:25–26 as “anyone” under negation; here أَحَدٌ positively names Allah as One, moving from no human match to God's absolute uniqueness.
The section says Iram's unmatched status is only created uniqueness and reserves true peerlessness for God; كُفُوًا أَحَدٌ says no equal belongs to Him.
The section states that created order is paired; خَلَقْنَا زَوْجَيْنِ makes the pair form a general feature of creation and says this should prompt remembrance.
The section's claim that created things come in pairs is stated as خَلَقَ الْأَزْوَاجَ كُلَّهَا, extending the pattern to plants, people, and what people do not know.
The section sets the paired created order against Allah's uniqueness; this ayah asks how He could have a child without a consort (صَاحِبَةٌ) when He created everything.
The section says creation is arranged in pairs; خَلَقْنَاكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا applies that form directly to human beings.
The section's root ش ف ع describes joining another as a supporter, then says people arrive alone; this ayah has them come فُرَادَىٰ and asks where their شُفَعَاءَ are, uniting both claims.
The section says each person finally comes without someone joined to their side; فَرْدًا states that everyone comes to God alone.
The section says the hoped-for support of an intercessor will not remain at judgment; شَفَاعَةُ الشَّافِعِينَ explicitly does not benefit the damned.
The section's root ش ف ع names support by interceding for another; this warning says no soul can avail another and no شَفَاعَةٌ will be accepted on the Day.
The section connects support for the orphan with intercession that will fail on the Last Day; this repeated warning likewise denies accepted شَفَاعَةٌ and says no soul will be helped.
The section's shafʿ branch is someone joining another as supporter; this Day has no trade, خُلَّةٌ (close friendship), or شَفَاعَةٌ, so even companionship cannot supply help.
The section says the person's hoped-for supporter will not accompany them at judgment; those warned of being gathered have no guardian or شَفِيعٌ besides God.
The section traces failed worldly care to being left without support; this ayah says the soul held for what it earned has no وَلِيٌّ or شَفِيعٌ besides God.
The section says there will be no one to join the condemned as an intercessor; at the unveiling of the promised outcome, they ask هل لنا من شفعاء and find none to speak for them.

The section says people who failed to support the vulnerable will themselves lack an intercessor; the people in the Fire lament, مَا لَنَا مِن شَافِعِينَ, and the next ayah adds that they have no intimate friend.
The section's lone person has no one to join their side; this continuation says there is no حَمِيمٍ (close friend), completing the lament of 26:100's absent intercessors.
At the trumpet, this ayah says kinship ties do not hold and people do not ask one another; it gives the section's arrival alone a concrete severing of family support.
As the section moves from the solitary soul to its final company, this Day-of-Resurrection scene has a person flee from his brother; the next ayat extend the flight to parents and family.
The section's account of a person without an earthly supporter meets this scene of fleeing from one's mother and father; 80:34 begins the list and 80:36 continues it.
The section's solitary arrival is echoed by a person fleeing wife and children; 80:34–35 begin the family list, and 80:37 says each is occupied with his own concern.
The section says everyone comes alone; this ayah concludes the fleeing-family scene by saying each person has enough concern of his own, completing 80:34–36.
The section says support will not pass from one person to another on the Day; this ayah states that no intimate friend will avail another and none will be helped.
The section's solitary return has a close parallel in a Day when no soul can do anything for another and all command belongs to God.
The section makes each person's final arrival individual; this Day is one when every soul pleads only for itself and is paid in full for what it did.
The section distinguishes support that truly joins a person from support that fails; this ayah reverses ordinary friendship at judgment, when friends are enemies except the God-conscious.
The section's root ر ض و is developed as two-sided satisfaction; on the Day truthful people benefit, Allah is رَضِيَ عَنْهُمْ and they are رَضُوا عَنْهُ.
The section hears reciprocal satisfaction in its paired forms; this ayah uses the same two-way رضو wording and places it with Gardens beneath which rivers flow.
The section's root ر ض و points to satisfaction between two parties; this ayah says Allah is pleased with the first believers and their followers are pleased with Him, then promises Gardens.

The section links رضى in two directions and glosses entering among God's servants as entering His party; this ayah says Allah is pleased with believers and they with Him, and calls them حِزْبَ اللَّهِ.
The section calls the orphan one left without a counterpart and needing someone to stand with them; this ayah recalls God finding the Prophet an orphan and sheltering him.
The section condemns failure to honor the orphan; this command فَأَمَّا الْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ turns that neglect into a prohibition on overpowering the vulnerable child.
The section says people fail to honor the orphan; this ayah describes the denier of judgment as يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ, repelling the orphan, making the failure visible.
The section's orphan is left without someone to join their side; this ayah calls reforming their affairs best and says that mixing lives with them is brotherhood, a direct form of joining.
The section says the orphan is not honored; this command protects orphans' property and forbids replacing good with bad, specifying material care.
The section's orphan needs someone to stand with them; this ayah requires testing orphans until maturity and delivering their wealth when they are ready.
The section reproaches withholding honor from the orphan; this command to show goodness to the orphan places that care among duties owed to God and neighbors.
The section makes support for the orphan the human form of joining another; these righteous people feed the orphan, poor, and captive despite loving the food.
The section's neglected orphan has no advocate; this warning says those who consume orphans' wealth unjustly are consuming fire, marking the boundary around exploitation.
The section's adjacent 89:18 condemns not urging food for the poor alongside neglecting the orphan; this ayah condemns failure to urge that feeding, completing 107:2's paired neglect.
The section moves from a soul addressed alone to being received among God's servants; God's address يَا عِبَادِ لَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْكُمُ الْيَوْمَ welcomes His servants on the Day without fear.
The section ends with entry among God's servants; this scene has the God-conscious brought to Paradise in groups and welcomed at its opened gates.
The section's final invitation joins a soul to God's servants; this ayah has the righteous enter Gardens with righteous parents, spouses, and descendants, extending reunion to family.
The section pictures a soul admitted among God's servants; the angels pray that God admit the righteous and their righteous parents, spouses, and descendants to Gardens.
The section turns solitary arrival into belonging among God's servants; in the Garden, God removes rancor and makes its inhabitants brothers facing one another.
The section's final entry gathers a soul into a community; this ayah says believing descendants are joined to their believing parents without diminishing anyone's deeds.
The section's entry among servants ends in belonging; after the group welcome of 39:73, the Garden's people praise God and say they may settle wherever they wish.
The section's soul enters a shared company after being summoned alone; the people of the Garden turn to one another in conversation, showing fellowship after judgment.
The section's dictionary gloss for entering among عِبَادِي is “among My party”; this ayah names حِزْبَ اللَّهِ as the group whose members prevail.
The section repeats the crushing of earth as دَكًّا دَكًّا; this Day's earth and mountains are crushed in دَكَّةً وَاحِدَةً, using the same root for one final blow.
The section says no one can bind as God binds; the command to seize and shackle the condemned begins that judgment scene, continued by fire and a long chain in 69:31–32.
The section pairs unmatched punishment with binding; this command sends the seized person into Hellfire, between the seizure in 69:30 and the chain in 69:32.
The section names God's unmatched binding; this scene specifies a chain seventy cubits long, completing 69:30–31's seizure and punishment.
The section pictures angels standing ṣaffan ṣaffa; this Day has the Spirit and angels standing in صَفًّا, adding their silence until the Most Merciful permits speech.
The section's صَفًّا صَفًّا stages angels in ranks; here all are presented before their Lord in صَفًّا, and the ayah recalls that they return as first created.
The section's yatim root marks one left without a matching protector; when asked where to spend, this ayah names orphans among the recipients, reversing abandonment through giving.
The section says an orphan should be honored and supported; this account of righteousness includes giving one's cherished wealth to orphans.
The section exposes the orphan's lack of support; this covenant commands good treatment of orphans alongside parents, relatives, and the needy.
The section reproaches neglect of the orphan; this inheritance rule directs that an orphan present receive provision and kind words.
The section says the orphan is left unhonored; this ayah makes fear of injustice toward orphans a condition for fair conduct.
The section's orphan needs someone to take their side; this ruling asks for justice to vulnerable orphan girls and forbids withholding what is due them.
The section says people fail to honor the orphan; this command forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best way until maturity.
The section's orphan is a person needing another's protection; this command likewise bars approaching orphan property except in the best manner until maturity.
The section links the orphan's aloneness with the need for someone to stand by them; the wall protects two orphans' treasure until they mature, by God's mercy.
The section shows care for the orphan as a human duty; this division of spoils assigns a share to orphans, making them recipients of communal provision.
The section connects neglect of the orphan to moral failure; this distribution names orphans among the recipients and prevents wealth from circulating only among the rich.
The section says a solitary orphan needs support; this account of the steep path names feeding an orphan who is a relative as a concrete act of care.
The section's root ش ف ع names one who joins another by intercession; this ayah makes intercession conditional, asking who can intercede except by Allah's permission.
The section says the hoped-for intercessor will not stand beside the person by right; here no شَفِيعٌ exists except after His permission.
The section's shafʿ branch is joining someone as supporter; worshippers call idols their شُفَعَاؤُنَا عِندَ اللَّهِ, exposing the hoped-for support that the section says fails.
The section's support branch of ش ف ع is bounded at judgment; this ayah says intercession is unavailable except to one holding a covenant with the Most Merciful.
The section says not everyone can join another as an intercessor; this ayah permits speech and intercession only for one allowed by the Most Merciful.
The section's supporter/intercessor can only join by God's leave; this ayah says the angels intercede only for those He approves.
The section says supposed supporters do not accompany their patrons at the end; this ayah says the partners will not be their شُفَعَاءَ and the patrons will reject them.
The section makes divine judgment the boundary of human support; this ayah says people have no وَلِيٍّ or شَفِيعٍ besides Him.
The section says intercession cannot supply a match for God's judgment; this ayah says intercession does not benefit except for one He permits.
The section's root ش ف ع includes a person joining another to help them; in the speaker's challenge, the gods' intercession would not avail him or save him.
The section says people hope for companions who will intercede; this ayah asks whether they have taken intercessors apart from Allah, setting up the answer in 39:44.
The section's root ش ف ع names advocacy on another's behalf; this answer says all intercession belongs to God, completing 39:43's question.
The section's solitary judgment leaves no supporter to join the person; this ayah warns of the approaching Day when no حَمِيمٍ or شَفِيعٍ is obeyed.
The section says there is no intercessor to join the condemned; this ayah says those invoked besides Allah do not possess الشَّفَاعَةَ, except a truth-witness.
The section's root ش ف ع marks help through intercession; the angels' intercession here cannot avail except after God's permission and approval.
The section says no supporter will accompany the person at judgment; this ayah says no close friend asks after a close friend, and the next ayat imagine relatives offered as ransom.
The section says the solitary person cannot count on a supporter; this continuation names brother as a ransom, with 70:10's unasked friend and 70:13–14 widening the loss.
The section's final aloneness is echoed by the wish to ransom one's clan; 70:10–12 establish failed friendship and family, and 70:14 makes the wish universal.
The section says no one can stand in for the person; this ayah imagines giving everything on earth to save oneself, completing the ransom list in 70:10–13.
The section says parents and children cannot keep a person from their own final return; this ayah states a father cannot avail his child nor a child his father on that Day.
The section depicts the singular arrival; this Day instead displays friends to one another while each is too occupied to ask after them, as 70:10–14 explains.
The section's root م ث ل means a peer or counterpart for Iram; here the same root appears in الْمَثَلُ الْأَعْلَىٰ, giving Allah the highest description.
The section distinguishes the unmatched Creator from paired creation; this ayah says multiple gods in the heavens and earth would bring ruin, marking the boundary of divine oneness.
The section says true unpaired uniqueness belongs to God; this ayah denies that He took a child or that another god is with Him, against a divided creation.
The section reserves unmatched sovereignty for Allah; this praise says He has no child or partner in dominion and no protector through weakness.
The section opposes created uniqueness to the One who creates; this ayah says Allah has no child or partner in dominion and created all things with measure.
The section contrasts paired creation with the uniquely One; this ayah rejects a son and closes by naming God الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ.
The section says the created world carries pairs; this ayah names two of each kind of fruit, making pairing visible in the earth's produce.
The section's general pair claim appears here in the created pairs and the ships and cattle made for riding.
The section says creation takes paired form; this ayah describes humanity from one soul and its mate, then the spread of men and women.
The section's pair image takes a social form here: God gives spouses from among people, then children and grandchildren.
The section connects pairing to mutuality; this ayah says spouses are made for tranquility and that affection and mercy are placed between them.
The section's claim that created order is paired is made concrete in two sheep and two goats within the eight kinds of cattle.
The section's paired order continues from sheep and goats to two camels and two cattle; this ayah completes the list begun at 6:143.
The section says created things come in pairs; this ayah specifies eight pairs of cattle within the creation and provision of humankind.
The section's pair theme appears in the creation of the male and female pair.
The section's pair theme appears again as God makes from the drop male and female.
The section's root م ث ل names Iram's counterpart; this ayah uses الْأَمْثَال for likenesses and warns not to set them up for God, preserving His unmatched status.
The section says no one inflicts punishment like God's; this ayah calls His punishment for the arrogant الْعَذَابَ الْأَكْبَرَ, a specific superlative parallel.
The section's dictionary branch for ي ت م calls a rare unmatched pearl “an orphan pearl”; this ayah names pearls among the two seas' bounty, though it does not call them rare.
